sections.label: Listening 1

items.stem: Which tool will the scientists use?
items.script: Our science team will record the temperature around the school. We discussed taking photographs and recording short interviews, but neither would help us organise the numbers. Our teacher has prepared a tablet with a special measuring app, so that is the device we will use.

items.stem: Where will the public workshop happen?
items.script: The museum is hosting an exhibition, and the library is busy with a reading competition. Because both buildings are full, the art workshop has moved to the community hall. A notice near the entrance gives directions and asks everyone to arrive ten minutes early.

items.stem: What transport did the visitors select?
items.script: Our visitors wanted to explore the old harbour. Taking a bus would have been cheap, while the train offered a quicker journey. However, the guide suggested travelling by traditional boat to see the coast from the water. Everyone agreed that this would be more memorable.

items.stem: Which object is going to be recycled?
items.script: In our technology lesson, we learned why electronic waste can harm the environment. My family still uses our old radio and desk lamp, but my damaged mobile phone cannot be repaired. I will take that phone to the school collection point tomorrow morning.

items.stem: Which plant did the group choose?
items.script: Students were asked to improve a sunny corner of the playground. A few suggested colourful flowers, and others wanted vegetables for the school kitchen. After speaking to the gardener, we chose a young tree because it could provide shade for future students.

sections.label: Listening 2

items.stem: The project started in October.
Only experienced adults were allowed to join a repair café.
The group received help from a local engineer.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly sixty people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Hind about a repair café. When did the project begin?
Hind: It began in October, when people in a community centre asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Hind: We started with testing electrical equipment. We were supported by a local engineer, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Hind: Not really. At one point, some parts could not be repaired. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on collecting spare parts for reuse. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Hind: I was happy when families saved money and materials. Nearly sixty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Hind: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Hind: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

sections.label: Reading 2
sections.passage:
When Hind heard about a repair café in a community centre, the idea sounded interesting but difficult. The project had started in October, and nobody was sure how many students would join. Hind decided to attend the first meeting anyway. At the beginning, the organisers explained why the project mattered to local people. They asked everyone to listen carefully before suggesting changes.

The group began by testing electrical equipment. Hind was worried about making mistakes, but a local engineer explained that learning through practice was an important part of the experience. After a few days, everyone had a specific responsibility. Some students recorded information, while others spoke to families who visited the area.

A difficulty appeared when some parts could not be repaired. The group could have stopped, but the students discussed several possibilities and chose a practical solution: collecting spare parts for reuse. They tested the idea, checked the results and made small changes where necessary. Instead of blaming anyone for the delay, they shared the work fairly.

At the end of the month, families saved money and materials. Hind felt confident and realised that a useful project does not need to be perfect on the first day. The students presented their work to the school council and suggested that another class could continue it next term. Hind kept a notebook with photographs and reflections, hoping it would encourage younger pupils to try something similar.

items.stem: Where is the interview taking place?
items.script: Our team has permission to interview a visiting writer this afternoon. We first considered the classroom, but another lesson will be held there. The garden might be noisy because of construction work nearby. We have booked a quiet corner of the library instead.

items.stem: What is the planned activity?
items.script: The student council wants an activity that encourages families to spend time outdoors. We thought about reading together and decorating classroom walls, but those could take place inside. We decided on a cycling event along the safe path near the sports centre.

items.stem: Which item should the visitor photograph?
items.script: For a local-history project, I must take a photograph of a place built many years ago. The modern office building is unsuitable, and the nearby bridge was completed only recently. The guide recommended the old castle, which has an interesting history and stone towers.

items.stem: What did the club order?
items.script: The student media club received money for one useful item. We already have a set of books and a shared tablet for writing articles. The members voted to purchase a camera so we could take clearer photographs during school events and exhibitions.

Only experienced adults were allowed to join a science podcast.
The group received help from his English teacher.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly eighty people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Faris about a science podcast. When did the project begin?
Faris: It began in September, when people in a school media room asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Faris: We started with interviewing a weather researcher. We were supported by his English teacher, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Faris: Not really. At one point, background noise spoiled the recording. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on moving to a quieter room. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Faris: I was happy when the episode reached many listeners. Nearly eighty people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Faris: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Faris: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.

items.script: At the school sports festival, the swimming pool will be closed for repairs and the football field is being prepared for next week. Visitors can still join a short running challenge around the track. Volunteers will give water to everyone who finishes.

items.stem: Which food is suitable for the demonstration?
items.script: Our nutrition group needs to prepare a meal without using electricity or a cooker. Baking a cake is not possible, and making soup would require heating water. We will prepare a fresh salad using vegetables from the school garden and explain its nutritional value.

items.stem: Which place will the researcher observe?
items.script: A university researcher wants to understand how people use open spaces. The museum has invited her to give a talk, and the hospital offered an interview. However, she will spend the morning observing visitors in the public park and recording their activities.

items.stem: Which weather problem delayed the trip?
items.script: Our environmental trip was postponed yesterday. It was sunny and there was no rain, so everyone was surprised. The organiser explained that strong wind made the boat journey unsafe. We will try again next weekend when the weather becomes calmer.

items.stem: Which instrument will be used?
items.script: The school concert will include several performers. The piano has already been booked for the opening song, and a group will play guitars later. For the final performance, our class needs a steady beat, so our music teacher has chosen a drum.

sections.label: Listening 2

items.stem: The project started in November.
Only experienced adults were allowed to join a wildlife monitoring project.
The group received help from a wildlife ranger.
The group solved its difficulty by buying expensive new equipment.
Nearly ninety people became interested in the project.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Young Voices. Today we are speaking with Dana about a wildlife monitoring project. When did the project begin?
Dana: It began in November, when people in a coastal nature reserve asked for something useful. Our group wanted everyone to take part, including students who had never volunteered before.
Interviewer: What was the first thing you did?
Dana: We started with counting birds without disturbing them. We were supported by a wildlife ranger, who showed us how to work safely and plan our time.
Interviewer: Was everything easy?
Dana: Not really. At one point, visitors sometimes left plastic waste. We listened to different suggestions before agreeing on placing recycling bins near paths. That helped us continue.
Interviewer: What was the most encouraging result?
Dana: I was happy when the beach became cleaner. Nearly ninety people became interested in what we were doing.
Interviewer: What is your advice to other students?
Dana: Start with a small idea. Ask questions, share responsibility and check whether your work is helping others. You do not need expensive equipment.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your experience.
Dana: Thank you. I hope more schools try similar projects next term.
